To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have used a combination of transposon insertion sequence and trait enrichment analysis to identify a large number of fitness determinants in a single ExPEC strain and that a significant proportion of these genes are found more often in pathogenic than non-pathogenic bacteria.

(1) Tn-seq in combination with zebrafish pathogenomics can be used to determine the fitness determinants of an ExPEC pathogen in vivo and (2) the Trait Enrichment algorithm is a useful tool to determine the phylogenetic conservation of candidate genes and to identify genes that are likely to be involved in virulence.
a novel Trait EnRichment Analysis (TEAR) algorithm was developed and used to identify genes with the potential for therapeutic and diagnostic use.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms by which bacteria cause disease, and how they adapt to different environments.
the identification of genes that contribute to bacterial pathogenesis and virulence.
the identification of novel virulence factors in a model ExPEC pathogen.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Tn-seq method is an extremely useful technique for identifying genes that are important for bacterial fitness, but that the method does not identify all of the genes that are important, and the TEA algorithm is a useful method for identifying genes that may be important for pathogenicity.
the combination of quantitative genetic footprinting with Trait Enrichment analysis is an efficient approach to identify fitness determinants of pathogenic organisms.

the approaches and observations presented herein provide a resource that can be utilized by future pathogenomics research and highlight the diverse factors required by a singular ExPEC isolate to endure within varying host environments.

The main takeaway from our work is that

Tn-seq, in conjunction with comparative genomics and Trait Enrichement Analysis, is a powerful approach to identify genes that promote bacterial fitness in specific host niches and that these genes may represent novel targets for therapeutic intervention.
the Tn-seq approach is highly complementary to comparative genomics and that TEA is a valuable tool for the identification of genes with a potential for therapeutic and diagnostic use.

the use of a combination of Tn-seq, TEA and zebrafish-based infection models can be used to identify genes that are important for bacterial fitness in a host environment, and that the genes identified by such approaches are more likely to be true virulence factors if their homologues have a higher frequency of occurrence in other pathogenic strains.
